en: Regarding the general dhāraṇī for the protection of the dharma common to all sections of the Tripiṭaka,
as transmitted by Vajrajñāna to his consecrated disciples:
whenever one wishes to perform recitation, one must first protect the body, establish the boundary, clarify the visualization, and contemplate the noble deity.

One who gives rise to a heart of compassion and takes pity on sentient beings, and makes great vows to dedicate [merit] toward Bodhi, may then perform the recitation as described in the sutras, employing it both at the beginning and the end.
If one first enters the maṇḍala, one should first bind the samaya seal and place it upon the crown of one's head;
then, universally prostrating before the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Great Compassionate Honored Ones of the three periods of time, one dedicates all accumulated roots of goodness.
With palms joined, one should rejoice in all [merit].

Reciting "Oṃ vajrapadma-vīju," and having thus performed the protective binding according to the ritual, if there are any transgressions of the samaya, one should confess all faults during the time of repentance by secretly reciting the *soma-vajra* mantra.

*Namo śrīvajreśvarāya sarvatathāgatānām āḥ hūṃ vīra vīra mahākrodhavajri sata sata sāradhe sāradhe trāye trāye vidhama ni-saṃjñani trāma ti-siddha-akṣaye ṭrīyaṃ svāhā.* The Samaya-mudrā of the Buddha Family: Join the two palms together at their sides; interlace the *kṣānti* (ring) and *dāna* (middle) fingers;
place the *vīrya* (forefinger) and *bala* (pinky) fingers upon the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhi* (little finger) respectively;
and bend and extend the *dhyāna* (thumb) and *prajñā* (index finger) so that they touch.
One should visualize the Honored Śākyamuni clearly present before one;
having formed the mudrā, with the crown of the head opened and spread, recite this secret mantra:

*Oṃ tathāgatodbhavāya svāhā*. Having recited it, place [the hands] upon the crown of the head and visualize that as this seal is perfected, he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, seated upon a lion throne of precious lotuses, and cause one’s own mental eye to clearly perceive all the Tathāgatas gathered at the summit of the head.
The Samaya-mudrā of the Lotus Family:
Joining the thumbs and wisdom-fingers together, with the tips of the middle fingers touching,
and spreading the ten fingers like a lotus— this should be performed like Avalokiteśvara.
Visualize [the deity] residing at the right side of the crown; one should perform the visualization in this manner. Recite this secret mantra: *Oṃ padmāmbavaye svāhā*.

Having recited it, place it at the right side of the crown, and immediately cause the mind’s eye to perceive Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, whose physical form is perfect and who is the color of deep red. He is fully adorned with a celestial crown, flower garlands, and various precious necklaces. Within his crown, a transformation Buddha sits upon a precious lotus flower in the gesture of preaching the Dharma. Furthermore, visualize the great bodhisattvas attending him like servants by the Buddha’s side, likewise attending the Tathāgata.
The Samaya-mudrā of the Vajra Family:
Place the samādhi and prajñā fingers back-to-back;
interlace the wisdom and dhyāna fingers by turning them over one another. This is called the Vajradhara.
Having completed the binding, place it upon the left side of the crown, identical to that of Vajradhara.
Recite this secret mantra:

"Oṃ vajrādhitiṣṭhāya svāhā. Having finished the recitation, place it on the left side of the crown and clearly visualize with the mental eye the Bodhisattva Vajradhara, whose body is the color of light green jade, holding a *vajra* and seated in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*). Furthermore, visualize immeasurable members of the Vajra family attending the Tathāgata.

Having bound the samaya, one should visualize that one's own body becomes entirely the syllable HŪṂ. Visualize this syllable as being the color of fire; from it, blazing flames arise, fiercely incinerating the three poisons and the secondary afflictions within the body until they are instantaneously and completely exhausted. At that time, the fire also subsides, leaving only the syllable HŪṂ, which melts into a bright moon situated within the heart.
When forming this visualization, one should not linger; swiftly turn the mind of wisdom to bring it to fulfillment.
The mudrā for the Immovable Vajra’s Dispelling of Obstacles:
Hold the two arms straight and upright as the vow-power, and form the square wisdom-hands like a hook-mudrā.
The Prajñāpāramitā hand is formed like a ring; the Samādhi hand is likewise.
Then, by means of the Kṣāntipāramitā hand, one pierces it into the center of the Prajñā palm.
This is called the Immovable Sword; use it to bind the boundaries of the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Drawing the sword, one circumambulates it to the right, expelling all māras. Recite the mantra: *Namaḥ samantavajrāya vajra-caraṇa mahā-ruṣaṇa sphoṭaya hūṃ trāṭ svāhā*.

Having recited it three times or seven times, perform three circumambulations to the right with the mudrā; this constitutes the protective binding (*rakṣā*). Performing three circumambulations to the left is called "expulsion" (*vidhūnana*). By the power of this mantra, one can provide great protection for the great boundary (*mahā-maṇḍala*) of the ten directions, as well as protect the person and purify the site; it can even defend the entire triple world, let alone a single location.

When one who practices this Dharma contemplates it in their mind, wherever the mantra and mudrā reach, they can cause all various species and classes of unruly malevolent spirits to see the blazing, wrathful Vajra like a great mass of fire pervading that entire place.

The power of this dharma is so vast that it is difficult to describe; even if one were to explain its efficacy extensively over many kalpas, it could not be exhausted. This is called the Immovable Vajra Dharma. Furthermore, this dharma also serves to bind and protect the five families, as set forth in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi Sūtra*.
The Seal of the Armor, Spear, and Helmet of All Tathāgatas:
Having first recited the secret mantra, rotate the fingers of the hands of effort (vajra-muṣṭi) around each other three times; then utter the syllable OṂ CAṂ.
Visualize the syllable Oṃ at the limbs of advancement and the syllable Khaṭa at the limbs of power;
imagine each as a blue cord, fastened like a suit of armor,
encircling and binding all the joints of the body.
Gradually reaching the crown of the head, it first descends from the *tān-hui* (wisdom-fist);
this is called the "Vajra Armor.
Recite this secret mantra:

"Oṃ vajrakavaca vajrakīla vajrāṅkuśa vajriṇa kaṃ. Having thus performed the binding, all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, shall see the practitioner as having a vajra body, clad in vajra armor, wielding a vajra-pestle, and abiding within the vajra realm; all demons, ghosts, and spirits will retreat, flee, and be unable to cause harm. This is called the "Armor and Spear Mudrā," as set forth in the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*.

Having performed these rites, one should again with utmost sincerity engage the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, visualizing prostrations to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas of the ten directions. With single-minded devotion, kneeling with hands clasped before an incense burner, one should visualize purifying the entire Dharma-realm. Furthermore, one should visualize this cloud of incense swirling to the right to form a pedestal, with clouds of flowers and exquisite fragrances draped everywhere; immeasurable jewel flowers arranged in rows and blooming, their fragrance rich and pervasive, serving as an offering to the Buddhas within each and every assembly.
While forming this visualization, recite this vidyā-mantra and repeat these verses:
"May these clouds of incense pervade the ten directions, And may the wondrous resonance of the songs fill the air.
I offer them to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, As well as to all Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas."
"I only pray that the Great Compassionate Honored One of the Three Realms will graciously bestow the sovereign power of samādhi.

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ svāhā khaṃ ugate saparāhime o o nāje svāhā.* Having recited this three times, one enters into all samādhis; whatever one contemplates according to one's mind shall be fully accomplished.

For one who performs this contemplation, desiring to cause the practitioner to eliminate the hindrance of afflictions and to purify both the internal and external body, one should further recite this Heart-Seal Dhāraṇī mantra to empower it.

"Oṃ sarvabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ sarvabhāvaśuddho ’haṃ. Having formed this thought, one utters the syllable *A*. Since this syllable *A* signifies non-arising—that is, that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally unborn—this gateway alone is able to distance one from defilements. When defilements are purified, there are no causes or conditions; when causes and conditions are absent, all phenomena are quiescent. Because all phenomena are quiescent, they are likewise the purity of the *tathatā* (suchness). Within this initial gateway, all meanings are complete; even the forty-two sages and worthies are likewise so.
The Samaya-mudrā of the Vajra Lower Direction:
Hold the *samaya* (vow) fingers upright and straight; interlace them with the backs turned toward the *praṇidhāna* (aspiration) fingers;
then, using the *samaya* fingers, insert them into the middle of the *darśana* (contemplation) wings.
The remaining fingers are each pressed together like a triangle.
Recite this secret mantra:

*Oṃ kili kili vajra-vajri bhura bhaṇḍa bhaṇḍa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having recited it, visualize that [the hand] becomes a single-pronged vajra, with flames extending downward to the adamantine limit (*vajrapratiṣṭhāna*). This rite can cause all the hosts of powerful evil māras in the lower direction to completely retreat and disperse.
The Vajra Four Directions Samaya Mudrā:
Without altering the previous mudrā, raise the dhyāna and prajñā fingers to form peaks;
circle them three times around the body, and this is called the Vajradhātu.
Wherever one’s mind intends to reach, it immediately becomes a boundary (dharmadhātu).
Recite this secret mantra:

*Oṃ śara śara vajraparākāra hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having recited it, perform the mudrā three times clockwise and brandish it; according to the distance intended by the mind, a wall-boundary is established. Immeasurable Vajras protect this boundary, causing those of non-affiliated classes to see it as a fierce flame, so that they flee in all directions like a great city of fire.
The Samaya Mudrā of the Vajra Above:
Without moving from the previous mudrā, place the thumb (dhyāna) on the side of the forefinger (agra-pada); the wisdom-finger (jñāna) is likewise.

"Oṃ viśvapralocchabuddharabhañjara muṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having recited this, raise the mudrā above the crown of the head and circumambulate three times; this will cause all evil demons, spirits, and various classes of heterodox beings in the upper direction to flee in terror, none daring to create obstacles.
The Seal of the Precious Chariot of All Noble Ones:
Concentration and wisdom are harmonized within; Vigor and power are established like mountain peaks;
Dhyāna is pressed at the side of the vow; Wisdom and patience are likewise so.
"Summoning all the worthy sages, The inner three invocations of dhyāna and wisdom— This is called the *āhvāna* (Invocation) mantra.

'Oṃ tūru tūru svāhā. Having recited this, one should visualize this precious chariot proceeding to the abode of the Sages. Upon this chariot, one visualizes a precious chamber adorning the maṇḍala; within that chamber is a precious lotus lion-throne, and upon the throne are immeasurable varieties of jewels used as adornments for the seated Sages. The Sages, filled with joy, arrive simultaneously in a single moment of thought."
The Seal for Summoning All Worthies and Sages:
Interlace the five fingers of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
place dhyāna above prajñā, aligning them upward toward the eyebrows; shape the fingers of vīrya and bala like hooks.
Three times he snaps his fingers; this is called the summons. Reciting "Oṃ vajrasamāja ja," at that time the summoned Bodhisattvas abide in the void.

Holding *gaṇḍī* drums and *vajra*s in their hands, they strike them to produce sound. That sound reaches afar to immeasurable worlds in the ten directions; all the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and all the Bodhisattvas, as numerous as motes of dust, all come to the assembly and stand before the practitioner. With minds already resolved, sincere and without doubt, because the Noble Ones joyfully and swiftly respond to their original vows, one then takes *argha* water to offer to the aforementioned Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas. One binds the *samaya* mudrā of the Buddha Family, holds the *argha* vessel, and recites the preceding Mantra for Purifying the Universal Dharma Realm three times.
Regarding the offering of *argha*: now, one offers pure and wondrous water to purify the locations of the Honored Ones, for the sake of the meaning of purity.
One establishes the mudrā of the holy flower-seat:
like the previous lotus mudrā, with the fingers slightly bent as if in full bloom.
Visualize a wondrous lotus flower and arrange seats according to their respective positions. Recite:

*Namaḥ samantamukhānām oṃ padmamālāye svāhā*. Having finished the recitation, visualize that the secret mudrā produces a wondrous lotus flower of brilliant color and fragrance; arrange these as seats for the various holy ones according to their positions.
He addressed him, saying:

"O Noble One, by the power of your original vow, you have not abandoned great compassion and have descended to this lowly and wretched place to open the mind toward the thought of the Uninterrupted Hell and other realms. I pray that you accept this meager offering; may you grant your empowerment so that the aspirations of all sentient beings may be fulfilled."
Next, recite the sublime verses to offer praise.
Form the mudrā of the Eight-Direction Fire Court:
Extend both palms flatly, with the wisdom hand placed above the concentration hand.
When meditative concentration and wisdom are raised straight up, it is called the Vajra Fire.

Having recited "Oṃ asamañji ni hūṃ," perform three circumambulations to the right with the mudrā; according to the distance intended by one's mind, it becomes like a great city of fire, causing all māras and obstacles to retreat, scatter, and flee.
Form the *samaya* seal of the ten directions of the celestial realms:
Interlace the fingers of concentration and wisdom within; join the tips of the patience and vow fingers together;
bend the advance and power fingers back against their backs, forming a shape like a three-pronged vajra.
The ritual manual for the *cāṇḍālī* [mudrā] states: "The *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.

Having recited 'Oṃ śaṅkari mahāsamaye svāhā,' perform three rightward swings [of the hand] to universally transform the eight directions, the four intermediate points, above, and below. Like the Great Pure Heaven (*Mahāśuddhadeva*), it becomes free from all defilement; within the secret assembly, it is vast, majestic, and pure. This is called the *samaya* rite."
Having thus performed the binding, the Sūtra states:
"Even if a Wheel-Turning King, the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa, or any other mantras that are contrary [to this], none shall find an opportunity."
Immediately, one offers various kinds of incense, flowers, food, and drink to the primary deity and the assembly of noble ones, and then makes aspirations and performs the dedication of merit.
As for the mudrā of the Family Mother (*kulamātṛ*) and the self-protection:
join the three fingers of wisdom (*prajñā*) with those of concentration (*samādhi*), and bend the index fingers (*vīrya*) like hooks.
Pressing the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhi* fingers against their backs so that they resemble the shape of the Buddha-eye (*buddhalocana*),
with the *dhyāna* and *jñāna* fingers held upright and opened, resting alongside the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhi*—
this is called the *kulamātṛ-mudrā*.

"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ tadyathā oṃ ruru saparu jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocani śaravara taśadani svāhā. Having recited this three times, one should encircle the noble deity with the mudrā; this is called the method for protecting the deity.
Furthermore, one should empower the four locations of one's own body with mantras and secret mudrās; this is called the Family Mother Samaya Rite.
Having thus performed the binding, one should recite according to the ritual at the four periods of each day, namely: early morning, midday, dusk, and midnight.
Holding four kinds of rosaries, one performs four types of recitation: first, vocal recitation;
second, vajra recitation, which is silent recitation performed by moving the tongue while keeping the mouth closed;
third, samādhi recitation, which is mental recitation.
Fourth is the true recitation, which consists of practicing according to the meaning of the syllables.

Whenever one wishes to recite, one must first bathe and perform the ritual protection (*rakṣā*) according to the rules. One should recite the *Kṣitigarbha* (Muṇḍarī) *hṛdaya-mantra* and consecrate water with it, sprinkling it upon one’s clothing. Regarding the water used for bathing: one should not kneel with the feet; rather, one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus flower to support the feet. Next, one should visualize that one’s own physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are identical to those of the Honored One (*devatā*).

When about to open the door, utter one sound of *HŪṂ*. Then, entering the maṇḍala, perform the liturgical repentance of the three karmas. Sequentially form the seals (*mudrā*) of the three samayas from the beginning. Next, hold the mantra of the deity and sit in either full or half-lotus posture as you prefer. Place both hands at the heart with a distance of one inch between them; by joining the beads together, form the seal for recitation. Continue until the limit is reached—whether ten thousand, one thousand eight hundred, four hundred, two hundred, or down to one hundred and eight. If the count is less than the above, it does not constitute valid recitation. During each session, you must not allow the mind to wander or engage in conversation with others. This is called the *Tattvasamaya* method of recitation.
Having finished the recitation, perform the confession once more and re-establish the eight offerings; then make vows according to one's heart’s desire, and they will all be accomplished.
Again, bind the samaya mudrā and release it sequentially until it is dispersed above the crown of the head.

Next, perform the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) and the fire-court boundary (*agnimaṇḍala-sīmā*). To release them, rotate [the hand] counter-clockwise. Furthermore, using the *ratha* mudrā as the summoning seal, flick it outward with the two fingers of wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditation (*dhyāna*); this constitutes the dismissal. Only after binding the protection of the body (*kāyarakṣā*) by means of the Mother of the Family (*kulamātṛ*) may you depart.

All devas shall behold this person as being identical to a noble one (*ārya*); no malevolent spirits or ghosts will dare to cause them harm; enemies and creditors will offer them respectful salutations with sincere hearts; and all sentient beings will benefit from them day and night. Therefore, the wise should settle their minds and practice the secret of this gateway: they should constantly practice giving, maintain compassionate concern for suffering sentient beings, and must not give rise to thoughts of anger or aversion. This is called the *samaya* recitation method.
Constantly visualize the syllable RAṂ upon the food to purify it; furthermore, visualize yourself as a three-pronged vajra and recite the Daśabala-mantra eight times before eating.
The mantra is: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyo oṃ vāyanti tejomaṇi svāhā*. The mantra of Kuṇḍalī is:
*Oṃ hulu hulu tiṣṭha tiṣṭha bandha bandha ha na ha na amṛte hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. The mudrā for the inner offering of the joyful play of all Tathāgatas:
The hands of śamatha and vipaśyanā are crossed externally; the dhyāna and prajñā fingers are held upright and parallel.

Holding them at the heart, one makes offerings to all the Tathāgatas. This is the mudrā for making offerings to Bodhisattvas; according to whichever Honored One one serves, may they swiftly grant their empowerment.
“Oṃ mahāratī. This is the mudrā for the inner offering of the *bodhimālā* (Buddha-garland) of all Tathāgatas:
With this mudrā of joyful play, extend the hands straight forward; this constitutes the *bodhimālā*, through which one prays to realize the awakening of the Tathāgata.
The mantra is: *Oṃ lu-pa-śu-vi*.
This is the mudrā for the inner offering of the vajra song of all Tathāgatas:
Form the previous mudrā and draw it down to the navel; gradually raise it up to the mouth and release it. Thus one offers the vajra song.
May one’s vow accord with the subtle and wondrous sound.
The secret mantra is:
Oṃ śrī-tārocca. This is the mudrā for the inner offering of the vajra dance of all Tathāgatas:
Each forms the vajra-fist; the dhyāna-hand is held facing the heart and pointing upward, while the jñāna-hand circles back and extends the *vara* and *prajñā* fingers;
together they rotate above the crown of the head and are then released. The mantra says:
"Oṃ sarvapuṣpe svāhā. This is the mudrā for the outer offering of incense to all Tathāgatas:
With the vajra-bond, release the fingers downward as if holding and burning incense; with clouds of Tathāgata-incense, make offerings throughout the entire dharmadhātu.
The mantra is: Oṃ praharaṇi. The mudrā for the external flower offering to all Tathāgatas:
Interlace the fingers of the dhyāna and wisdom hands with their palms facing outward, then scatter them upward; [this represents] clouds of subtle and wondrous flowers.
Universally hold the offerings with a focused mind. The mantra is:
"Oṃ phalaka me. This is the mudrā for the external offering of lamps to all Tathāgatas.
Immediately, with the vajra-bind, one should press the dhyāna and prajñā fingers together; holding the lamp of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, one universally illuminates all activities.
The secret mantra says:
"Oṃ sustirjaḥ. This is the mudrā for the outer offering of perfumed unguent to all Tathāgatas:
With the vajra-bind at the heart, open the fingers as if applying unguent; holding this sublime sandalwood, offer it like clouds of oceans.
The mantra is: "Oṃ su-kaṃ-daṅ-ni.

Having thus completed the offerings and praises, one should contemplate the samādhi of the *iṣṭadevatā* so that the mind does not wander. The yogin, empowered by the various seals (*mudrā*) of the vajra body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, further visualizes his own body as being fully adorned with all the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). Thereupon, he should recite the hundred-syllable mantra of the Mahāsamaya-mudrā to make his body firm, and then bind the Samaya-mudrā of the *iṣṭadevatā*.
The Samaya-mudrā of Vairocana’s Dharmakāya:

Interlace the outer fingers of the wisdom and meditation hands; extend the thumbs and ring fingers upright and slightly bent; place the index and middle fingers on the back [of the hands], keeping their three joints straight and upright.
The mantra is the Hundred-Syllable Vidya.

Because it is empowered by the Mahāśīta Hundred-Syllable Mantra, even if one has committed the sins of immediate retribution or slandered all Buddhas and the Vaipulya sūtras, the practitioner of mantra—by means of the deity’s firm abiding within his own body—shall attain in this very life all sought-after *siddhis*, namely the most supreme *siddhi*, the Vajrasattva *siddhi*, and even the Tathāgata’s most supreme *siddhi*. Without altering the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Vajradhātu, one should recite the root mantra of the deity:
With the two hands of Samādhi and Prajñā holding a rosary, Having recited the original mantra seven times, as before,
Raising [the visualization] to the crown of the head and again to the heart, one should remain steadfast in meditative equipoise (*samādhi*) while reciting.
With the tip of the tongue moving slightly and the lips and teeth closed, one contemplates the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) by following them up and down the body.
One should practice diligently at all four times of day without interruption, setting a limit of a thousand or ten hundred recitations, or even exceeding that.
All supernatural powers, merits, and wisdom—may one manifest in this very life as the All-Illuminating Honored One.

Once the practitioner has completed the allotted time for recitation, they should hold the *mālā* upon the crown of their head and earnestly make great vows. Thereafter, they should form the *samādhi-mudrā*, enter the *dharmadhātu-svabhāva-samādhi*, and practice the Five-Syllable *Svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*.
All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; their intrinsic nature transcends verbal expression.
Pure and free from defilement, they are like space due to karma and other factors.
Turning back to contemplate them with discernment, every syllable and word is true.
Though there are distinctions between the beginning and the end, all that is produced returns to oneness.
Without abandoning this samādhi, one dwells simultaneously in objectless compassion,
universally wishing that all sentient beings may be no different from oneself.
Once the practitioner has emerged from samādhi, they should immediately form the root mudrā and recite the root mantra seven times.

Furthermore, they should make offerings to all the Buddhas, praising and extolling them with sublime words and phrases, and present *argha* water. Then, using the "Descending upon the Three Times" mudrā, they should rotate it counter-clockwise to dissolve the boundary. Immediately forming the Vajra Liberation mudrā, they should bid farewell to the holy ones, each returning to their own original land.
Form the previous samaya-mudrā; with the thumbs and ring fingers supporting the flower, bring it to the crown of the head and scatter it. The mantra is:

"Oṃ kṛtobaddhasattvavīrya siddhyadhitiṣṭha āgaccha gacchatvaṃ buddhavisayānuparāgamanaodyo oṃ mañjūsattvamūḥ. Having performed this rite, once again recite the empowerment mantra with the Samaya-mudrā and seal the four places [of the body]. Then, receive the empowerment and don the adamantine armor (*vajrakavaca*). Following the previous procedure, perform the four prostrations to the Buddhas of the four directions, engage in confession, make aspirations, and so forth. Subsequently, in a secluded and quiet place adorned with incense and flowers, recite the Mahāyāna sūtras while abiding in the samādhi of the Principal Deity (*mūlamantra*), and practice walking meditation as desired.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this teaching, And practice with diligence throughout the four periods of day and night,
They shall realize the Stage of Joy in the present life, And after sixteen lifetimes, attain perfect enlightenment.
The General Mudrā for Purifying the Rosary of All Families:

With both hands in the lotus-palms gesture, join the tips of the earth-touching and wish-granting fingers; let all the remaining fingers touch one another, slightly opening them in the manner of a blooming flower.

Having formed this mudrā with the mantra "Oṃ vasuvati śrīye svāhā," one should take up the rosary, hold it in the left hand, and recite it seven times; this is called the "Pure Rosary-Holding Mudrā" common to the five families.

When reciting mantras: if one belongs to the Buddha Family, hold the beads with the *jinyi* (vīrya) fingers; if one belongs to the Vajra Family, hold them with the *renyuan* (kṣānti) fingers; if one belongs to the Lotus Family, hold them with the *jiefangdu* (śīla) fingers. This briefly clarifies the essential methods for recitation in the three families; the Ratna and Karma Families shall be explained separately later.
Regarding the general method for using a rosary: place both hands at the heart with the palms one inch apart; by holding the beads between them, the recitation is accomplished.
This method is explained in detail within the Yoga Tantras.

Furthermore, regarding the method received from the ācārya, it differs slightly from the previous one: simply by placing the palms of wisdom (prajñā-pāṇi) horizontally and facing upward, with the wings of concentration (samādhi-pakṣa) covering them, and bringing the tips of the fingers together as if holding a rosary, the ten pāramitās are thereby accomplished.
When reciting mantras, one should perform offerings such as burning incense, scattering flowers, presenting lamps, and applying fragrant ointments.

"Oṃ vajra dhūpe āḥ. The mantra for scattering flowers is:
"Oṃ vajrapuṣpe oṃ. The mantra for offering lamps is: "Oṃ vajraloke.
The mantra for scented unguents is: "Oṃ vajragandhe.
Even if one cannot procure other items, these six kinds of substances—scented unguents, flowers, incense, food, lamps, and *homa* offerings—must not be lacking.

Next, one should visualize that this incense smoke becomes a cloud-pavilion of five-colored light, spreading and filling all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time. It produces various kinds of music, emitting wondrous sounds of song and hymn to offer praise; it creates various kinds of exquisite fragrances such as sandalwood and aloeswood; it creates various kinds of delicacies, medicinal decoctions, and superior flavors; it creates various kinds of clothing, necklaces, flowing springs, and bathing pools of superior tactile qualities; and it creates various kinds of dhyāna-concentration, wisdom, and pure, true dharmas of immeasurable gateways. All these completely fill the Dharma-realm to perform Buddha-work, making offerings to all Buddhas and the Triple Gem of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and gathering in and perfuming all sentient beings so that they may resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
Before each and every Buddha, he saw his own body making such offerings, all identical and without distinction.
Furthermore, he made this vow:
"May all sentient beings enter the ocean of my dharma-realm."

Once this mindfulness is established, one immediately prostrates with the five limbs touching the ground and declares aloud:

The Ritual Procedure for the Sequence of Samādhi Offerings: Regarding the ritual procedure for the sequence of samādhi offerings, whenever one wishes to perform recitation, one first forms the samaya-mudrā and places it upon the crown of one’s head. Each of these mudrās is produced from the various limbs and joints of the bodies of all Tathāgatas, adorned with the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). For each Tathāgata, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of mudrās, and each mudrā has its own immeasurable retinue.

I shall now briefly explain the differentiation of seals arising from a single seal: according to the application of various dharmas, a single mantra gives rise to all mantras. If one were to explain this extensively as it is disseminated in practice, it would be immeasurable; there is no need for further elaboration.

Why is this? I have already provided detailed explanations in other sections; as for the Vinaya rules and the mantras and mudrās of accomplishment taught in the three classes of tantras, one may freely select and employ them from among them all.
A practitioner should not eat anything foul or impure; one should not eat leftover food from previous nights, for if one does so, one will not realize *siddhi*.

One should not even eat food offered to the Buddhas or Bodhisattvas, nor should one eat things that are green, black, or otherwise unsuitable. Furthermore, one must not sit upon, lie upon, or eat while seated upon the beds of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or those of one’s preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), parents, and so forth. Moreover, one must not speak while eating, nor pass food between people using the same vessel. These matters have been extensively analyzed by me in accordance with the teachings of the Vinaya.
Such dharmas as these have been briefly explained in summary; if I were to dwell for vast eons wishing to expound them, they would be inexhaustible.
As for the vessels used for eating, they consist purely of red and white copper trays and the like; furthermore, one does not rub the teeth with the hands.

The mantra-practitioner should know that he must sit upright in the full lotus posture and eat in silence according to the Dharma; he must not go to the homes of the deceased, families where a birth has recently occurred, impure households, or the homes of caṇḍālas, nor should he offer or consume leftover, stinking, or stale food.

Three times each day, one should vow to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Great Bodhisattva Saṃgha; arouse the bodhicitta; purify the three karmas; and contemplate the six recollections—namely, those of the Three Jewels, ethical discipline, generosity, and the devas—and so forth. With a single mind, one should practice the pure brahmacarya, remaining unlike the non-Buddhists. One should keep the hair and nails clean and trimmed; for if the hair grows long, lice and nits will arise, which in turn give rise to various obstacles and faults. Long hair requires much effort for combing and washing, and it diminishes the frequency of one’s recitations and chants.

If one's hair is long, nails are sharp, or filth and impurities are retained within, the handling of incense or the burning of it will result in defilement and contact, giving rise to obstacles and faults accordingly.
One must not observe or discuss eclipses of the sun or moon, nor should one revile or slander one’s Upādhyāya or Ācārya.

If one sees a land that is without a ruler and in a state of chaos, one must by no means dwell therein to practice the dharma or perform recitations. One must not dwell in lands protected by gods or nāgas; lands where yakṣas and rākṣasas constantly gather and reside; śmaśānas where the Buddha-dharma does not exist; lands inhabited by tigers and wolves; lands with many mosquitoes and gadflies; lands in regions where it never rains or where there is much wind; lands with many bandits; lands where slaughter occurs; lands where wine is sold; lands where scriptures and images are sold; lands where weapons for violence are sold; lands of courtesans; and lands where many people congregate. One must not dwell in any of these places to conduct dharma practices or recitations, for in all such cases, nothing will be accomplished.

One should skillfully discern that among all classes of recitation, this method is the most extensively accomplished; small effort yields small accomplishment. When performing the ritual of invocation, during recitation, or when practicing any rite for the fulfillment of wishes, one should sever all speech, whether wholesome or unwholesome.

Seated in the full lotus posture at the place of recitation, one should visualize all sublime dharmas forming a river of fragrant water in which one’s body is submerged and bathed. Sealing the body with mantras and mudrās, one should regard oneself as a Buddha, Bodhisattva, or similar being, with fragrant ointments smeared over the entire body. During all recitations, one must not shake the body or engage in restless observation or listening. If there is breaking of the posture, shaking, or coughing, one should immediately perform the *punar-maṇḍala* (renewal) by binding the bathing mudrā and sealing the body. Holding pure water, one should wash the hands and rinse the mouth, then perform the recitation according to the dharma to achieve extensive accomplishment; small effort yields small accomplishment.

According to the attainment of the superior, middling, and inferior levels of realization, there are generally three types of goals sought: first, for the sake of accomplishing mantras; second, for the sake of extinguishing transgressions and acquiring merit; and third, for the sake of future results.

*vajradhūpa* incense, *vajrapuṣpa* flowers, *vajradīpa* lamps, and *vajragandha* unguents.
The above are the four kinds of external offerings.

"Oṃ bhiḥ bhiḥ piśācānāṃ huṃ bhūtānāṃ svāhā. At that time, from the world established by the Vajra-wheel, the Blessed One visualized the syllable *yaṃ* arising from the Vajra-realm to form the wheel of the world—namely, the earth-wheel, the wind-wheel, and the space-wheel—all of which were entirely black in color.
Again, visualize the syllable *khaṃ* forming the Vajra Encircling Mountains, purely adorned with various jewels.

Furthermore, within the wheel of space, visualize the syllable *bhrūṃ* as Vairocana Buddha. From the navel of Vairocana Buddha, a universal stream of great compassionate nectar flows forth, forming a sea of nectar that fills the wheel of the Dharma-realm of space. Within this sea, again visualize the syllable *pra*; this syllable transforms into the shape of a tortoise, its shell golden in color, its body vast and immeasurable yojanas in extent.

Upon the back of the tortoise, one further visualizes the syllable *hrīḥ*. This syllable transforms into a magnificent yellow lotus, with a brilliant red blossom; the flower has three tiers and eight petals, complete with a pedestal and filaments. Furthermore, upon the flower’s pedestal, one visualizes the three Brahma-syllables—*praṃ*, *hūṃ*, and *baṃ*—which constitute Mount Sumeru, composed of various jewels and possessing eight faces.
Visualize five Brahma-syllables upon the summit of that mountain; these then become a great palace.

The palace is square with four gates complete on all sides, flanked by auspicious banners to the left and right, and surrounded by railings and four tiers of stairways. Above the palace is a five-peaked pavilion, adorned with hanging variegated silks, pearl nets, and flower garlands interwoven and draped about it.

Furthermore, above the four corners outside the hall and at the corners of the various gates, they were adorned with alternating arrangements of vajra-jewels. The eaves and steps of the hall were further embellished with various jeweled bells, chimes, gongs, rings, and pendants that reflected one another; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced harmonious and clear sounds. Precious banners and necklaces filled the air, and the space was exquisitely decorated with subtle fragrances and diverse flowers.

Furthermore, outside of that, there are immeasurable kalpa-trees arranged in variegated rows; the celestial beings compete in playing exquisite music and singing hymns, while the lords of the asuras, mahoragas, and others perform sublime songs and dances.
Within that palace is a maṇḍala, adorned with eight vajra-pillars. In the supreme and wondrous wheel of the Tathāgata family, there are three Brahma-syllables:

one should visualize the syllable *HŪṂ* in the center, and the syllable *A* on the left and right. These three syllables then transform into a lion throne, adorned on all four sides, most subtle and sublime.

Within the Vajra Family, one should visualize three Brahma-syllables: the syllable GA at the center, with the syllable HŪṂ on both the left and right. These three syllables transform into an elephant throne, adorned on all four sides, the most exquisite and sublime of all.

Within the Ratna family, there are three Brahma-syllables; in the center is the syllable *sa*, and one should visualize the syllable *tra* on the left and right. From these syllables, a horse-seat (*aśvāsana*) is transformed, adorned with the seven treasures on all four sides, being the most exquisite and supreme.

Within the Lotus Family, there are three Brahma-syllables: in the center is the syllable *maṃ*, and on both the left and right is the syllable *hrīḥ*. These three syllables transform into a peacock throne, adorned on all four sides with vajra-lotus jewels, which is the most exquisite and supreme.

Within the Karma-varga, there are three Brahma-syllables: in the center is the syllable *khaṃ* (剣), and on both the left and right are the short *a* (阿). These three Brahma-syllables transform into the seat of the Garuḍa, which is adorned throughout its four sides with jewels, being the most exquisite and supreme.

At that time, once the Tathāgata had sat upon the fivefold seat, together with the sixteen great bodhisattvas, as well as the four pāramitās, the four kinds of internal offerings, the four kinds of external offerings, the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*), and the four bodhisattvas, all remained in their fundamental *samādhi*. Each visualized their respective distinct seals (*mudrā*) and signs; these phenomena and characteristics all emerged from the body and mind of Vairocana Tathāgata.

Furthermore, one contemplates that upon each of the five thrones there is a lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*), within which is a most exquisite lotus pedestal with a full and perfect calyx. After these Tathāgatas have sat upon these seats, before long they attain equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and fully realize the mind of Samantabhadra of all Tathāgatas.

Furthermore, he was consecrated upon the crown of his head with the great maṇi jewels produced from the space of all Tathāgatas; he attained the dharma-knowledge of Avalokiteśvara of all Tathāgatas, the ultimate pāramitās, and the completion of all functional applications; and he achieved the wisdom of skillful means for the unimpeded activities of all Tathāgatas.
Because the practitioner contemplates yoga in this manner, they immediately give rise to vajra-wisdom.

By means of this wisdom, they are able to fully comprehend and realize all activities performed in the past, future, and present; furthermore, regarding the meanings of hundreds of thousands of Mahāyāna words and phrases never before seen or heard, they spontaneously awaken to and understand them all.
Regarding the method of visualization for making aspirations: if one seeks non-conceptuality, one should visualize non-conceptuality and the absence of mental recollection;
if one seeks the signless and formless, one should visualize syllables and the absence of syllabic recollection;
if one seeks the gate of non-duality, one should visualize one's two arms.
If one seeks the four immeasurables, one should contemplate the four arms;
if one seeks the six supernormal powers, one should contemplate the six arms;
if one seeks the eightfold noble path, one should contemplate the eight arms.
If one seeks to fulfill the ten pāramitās and the ten bhūmis, one should visualize ten arms;
if one seeks to become a Tathāgata who universally responds to the world, one should visualize twelve arms;
if one seeks the thirty-two marks of a great man, one should visualize thirty-two arms.
If one seeks the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, one should contemplate the eighty-four arms.

Through such contemplation as described above, one shall enter the profound, vast, and inconceivable stage of the samādhi-gates of all Tathāgatas; this is the station of right mindfulness, this is right suchness, and this is right liberation.
On the first day of beginning the recitation, when entering the maṇḍala: if performing the maṇḍala for pacification (śāntika), begin the ritual at sunset;
if performing the maṇḍala for increase (pauṣṭika), begin the ritual at sunrise;
if performing the maṇḍala for subjugation (ābhicāruka), begin the ritual at midday.
If one performs the rite for subduing enemies, one should begin the ritual at midnight.
However, for all maṇḍalas, the ritual is generally begun at sunset; among the various methods of recitation, this particular method is the most supreme.
If one deviates from this time, success will certainly not be achieved.

However, for all maṇḍalas, one must not begin the rite during the day, as it will result in great suffering; nor should one perform the ritual at midnight, for by deviating from the prescribed time, various obstacles will arise. All other times should be understood accordingly.

During the first watch of the night, when all affairs are tranquil, ritual practices become efficacious; the devas assemble and bestow their blessings upon the practitioner as they observe the rite. If one invokes the honored deities, they will descend immediately to fulfill one's requested aspirations. The wise should understand that this is the appropriate time for performing rites of auspiciousness, enrichment, and other such activities.

However, for all maṇḍalas, one begins the ritual at the time of sunset; before the first light of dawn appears, one must certainly conclude it. I shall now briefly explain the three types of places for accomplishing *siddhi* and the signs of accomplishment. As for those that do not lead to accomplishment: first, a place where there is a wicked king; second, a place with many thieves; third, a place with evil companions, famine, and so forth—in these places, one should never dwell to practice the Dharma together.

Furthermore, there are three times during which ritual acts should not be performed: namely, during extreme cold, during torrential rain, and during extreme heat; in such times as these, one is incapable of performing ritual acts.

Furthermore, there are three periods during which it is appropriate to practice the Dharma; one should skillfully discern and know them: from the fifth watch until the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), from the hour of the Horse (11 a.m.–1 p.m. until the hour of the Sheep (1–3 p.m.), and from the hour of the Rooster (5–7 p.m. until the hour of the Boar (9–11 p.m.). During such times, if one performs extensive recitation, one will fully accomplish the visualizations and practices of the maṇḍala.

Therefore, you should know that I possess a hidden intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) endowed with all the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), which is not within the sphere of your knowledge; for this reason, it is called the Secret Treasury of the Great Maṇḍala Teachings.
To briefly explain the characteristics for selecting the site: before sunrise, dig the ground three feet deep; one shall then see what object is there.
If it is in the likeness of a human, the power of one's mantras can shatter mountains and cover the seas;
if it is in the likeness of a beast, that too is auspicious.
If one sees jade, that person was among those present at the initial assembly;
if one obtains gold, that person shall, through wisdom, attain great wealth and nobility;
if one obtains items such as swords, staves, bows, or arrows, they have seen the mantra-deities within the altar.
If one obtains medicine, it can effectively eliminate illness;
if one obtains iron or stone, that person will lack firmness;

if one obtains bone, it is an inauspicious sign. One must immediately perform repentance and receive the precepts, then select a pure site, dig three feet deep, remove the impure soil from within, and separately take pure earth, pounding it with fragrant powder and tamping it down firmly.
Next, the method for the timing of the accomplishment of the Great Dharma is explained.

If one performs the rite in the first month, it will certainly be free of obstacles. If performed in the second month, various obstacles will certainly manifest. If performed in the third month, there will certainly be wind and clouds. If one begins the rite on the fifteenth day of the fifth month, rain will certainly fall. If the rite is performed in the ninth month, thunder and lightning will certainly appear.
In all ritual procedures (*vidhi*), when these conditions are present, success is certain; this the practitioner should know.

Whether for seven days, thirteen days, or twenty-three days—should one obtain a day under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), it is even more excellent—or during an eclipse of the sun or moon, these times are likewise foremost.

If one wishes to accomplish the dharmas of peace and security, one should employ the second and third months for the rite of abundance, and the tenth and eleventh months for the rite of subduing enemies.

Regarding the fourth and fifth months, I shall now briefly indicate: at a great famous mountain, a place inhabited by sages, or in a hermitage cave, or in a solitary new room, dwelling alone among forests and springs; in such places that are single-mindedly empty, tranquil, secluded, and excellent; or again, in a quiet location on a mountain peak, or within an araṇya, or inside a mountain cave, or in a monastery, or in a grove, or by a river or the bank of a stream, or at a site where sages previously dwelt—in these places, one will quickly achieve accomplishment.

The mandala for dispelling calamities and extinguishing sins should be made circular with a wheel at its center; the mandala for seeking aspirations should be made square with a lotus at its center; the mandala for following specific rites should be made triangular with a three-pronged trident at its center; and the mandala for seeking love and affection should be made like a lotus leaf with the syllable HŪṂ at its center.
When a yogin practices samādhi, he should follow the Buddha’s essential instructions for recitation.
If he contemplates the Tathāgata Vairocana, he first visualizes an eight-petaled lotus, imagining that the syllable *A* transforms into a lion throne, upon which is a white lotus.

Furthermore, one contemplates that the syllable *vaṃ* transforms into a stūpa, which changes into the primary deity Vairocana. His body is golden like the Jambūnada gold; his neck is adorned with blazing flames, he wears light celestial robes, and he bears a five-Buddha crown. His exquisite radiance shines brilliantly throughout the human, deva, and triple worlds. He summons the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the ten stages; because they have received empowerment, they manifest in form bodies, their forms adorned with precious necklaces, abiding in the sublime Samādhi of Form. Desiring to transcend the physical appearances of all the devas, he dwells within a circle of light and recites the secret mantra:

"Avira hūṃ khaṃ. First, the practitioner visualizes Vairocana Tathāgata within the heart of his own body. He imagines a letter *A*, like the full moon, emitting white light; the Tathāgata sits upon a white lotus flower therein, his body the color of vermilion gold, and he then binds the fundamental samaya-mudrā.

Having formed the vajra-fists with both hands, one should extend the middle fingers and hold them as if gazing at them; by means of this mudrā, one is able to receive from all Buddhas the prediction of attaining *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, the practitioner should contemplate Vairocana seated in the vajra-posture within the maṇḍala, his marks and signs complete, endowed with great majestic power, his physical form as bright white as the pure full moon, his entire body composed of radiant light. Adorned with a jeweled crown, his braided hair falls over his shoulders, and he is clothed in celestial garments of light and subtle silk. Through the secret wheels of the three karmas—body, speech, and mind—he manifests miraculous transformations; thus the practitioner should reflect.
The mantra is: *Oṃ vajradhātu hrīḥ*.

If one performs the recitation for the samādhi of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one should visualize the syllable *Hrīḥ* within a lotus; the radiance of that syllable is like that of a lotus, emitting various rays of light that transform into Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. His body is brilliantly radiant, the color of a red lotus, and within the topknot on his head is the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja. His body is adorned with a jeweled crown and necklaces; in his left hand he holds a blue lotus at his heart, and his right hand is as if plucking a lotus petal.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the gate of samādhi as being like a lotus flower, which is unsullied by dust or water and cannot be defiled or burdened by the stains of craving.
Having thus completed the contemplation, the heart-mantra for the visualization of the Honored One Avalokiteśvara is recited:

*Oṃ vajradharma hrīḥ*. If performing the recitation of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, one visualizes the syllable *Hūṃ* within a lotus flower. His body is the color of gold, his head has five topknots, he holds a blue lotus in his meditation hand and a Prajñā-pāramitā manuscript in his wisdom hand, and he sits within a moon disc surrounded on four sides by vajras. The Holy One is seated upon a multicolored jewel-flower in the midst of this, emitting red light. He then speaks the Heart-Mind Mantra:

"Oṃ vajratīkṣṇa-dhāra svāhā. If one contemplates the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, one should visualize the syllable *tra* within the center of a lotus pedestal. This transforms into a red crystal jewel with flames pervading all around, which then becomes the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja. His body is the color of purple gold, and he bears the five Buddhas upon his crown. His left hand bestows fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), and his right holds a blue lotus; within the flower is a red crystal jewel. The Bodhisattva sits upon this blue lotus in the midst of a moon disc. Recite the mantra as follows:

"Then, for one who recollects Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, one should visualize the syllable *su-ba* within the center of a lotus pedestal; this transforms into a golden knife, which becomes Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. His body is the color of the moon, and his crown is adorned with the five Buddhas, their majestic radiance blazing like the solar disc. The Bodhisattva sits therein upon a thousand-petaled lotus, emitting light of various colors, seated within a lunar disc and completely surrounded by three-pronged *vajras*. One should then recite the mantra as follows: *Tadyathā | oṃ ariga-ma-ri-mu-ri svāhā*."

"Then, *Samantavajra Hūṃ*. If one contemplates the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, one should visualize a single syllable *Hūṃ* within the center of a lotus pedestal. This transforms into a *vajra*, which becomes the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha. His body is the color of light green jade; he wears the five Buddhas upon his crown; his meditative hand is formed into a vajra-fist placed at his heart; and his wisdom hand holds a *vajra* emitting flames of light. The Noble One sits thereupon a precious lotus flower, surrounded by three ancient *vajras* encircling a lunar disc. Recite the mantra as follows:

"Vajrasattva Asvāhā. If the Bodhisattva Cintāmaṇicakra performs recitation, he should visualize the syllable *Vrīḥ* within the center of a lotus pedestal. This transforms into a *cintāmaṇi* jewel, exquisitely variegated and like a sun disk emitting great radiance. It further transforms into the Bodhisattva Cintāmaṇicakra, his color like refined gold, wearing Amitāyus Buddha upon his crown, endowed with six arms and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). The Bodhisattva manifests transformations throughout the six realms of existence, enabling sentient beings to fulfill the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). He dwells on Mount Potalaka, contemplating samādhi, and so forth.

When the Bodhisattva Tārā performs recitation, she visualizes the syllable *ṇa* within a lotus; this transforms into a blue lotus, which becomes the Bodhisattva Tārā. Her body is flesh-colored, adorned with various ornaments, and upon her crown is the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja. Her left hand holds a blue lotus at her heart, while her right hand bestows fearlessness to fulfill all wishes. Within this, the Noble One rides upon a precious lotus, emitting white light that can fulfill all aspirations; it is called "Accordance with the Mind" (*Cittānugā*). The mantra is as follows:

"Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā. At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of Universal Radiance Tārā. By the power of this samādhi, he emitted a great light from the pupil of his right eye within his countenance; from the flow of that light, the form of a sublime maiden appeared. She abided in the Samādhi of Exquisite and Sublime Color, her body adorned with priceless various jewels, and she was surrounded before and behind by immeasurable devas.

First, visualize the syllable *Oṃ* at the crown of the head; next, visualize the syllable *Hūṃ* on the forehead; place the syllable *Ṭa* within the pupils of both eyes; again, establish the syllable *Hūṃ* at the throat; then, place the syllable *Li* upon both shoulders; visualize the syllable *Ṭa* again at the heart; if [the deity resides] in the navel, visualize the syllable *Li* there; visualize the syllable *Svaḥ* between the two hips; and again, visualize the syllable *Ha* upon the shins. Having thus arrayed these syllables throughout the body, one may then invite the Principal Deity to enter the ritual body (*dharmakāya*). For this reason, one first performs the visualization and subsequently makes the invitation.

Regarding the visualization of the Vajra-samaya: the practitioner visualizes within the moon disc of the heart a syllable *HŪṂ*. This *HŪṂ* transforms into five *vajra-gadās*, which are made of pure gold like a mass of molten, refined gold, emitting red light like a blazing conflagration. This radiance is magnificent and pervasive throughout the body; with the vajra-wheel of body, speech, and mind, it pervades the realm of birth and death. Within the measure of a full moon, it manifests miraculous transformations; the size of this vajra-wheel is not fixed, being commensurate with the full moon disc.

Whether visualizing five ancient [deities], three ancient ones, or a single ancient one, one may do so at will without obstruction. From the pores and joints of one’s own body, vajras as numerous as motes of dust appear; from within each vajra, various types of bodies can further emerge, enabling the practitioner to subdue beings according to their inclinations, and allowing for the accomplishment of all dhāraṇī-gates and samādhi-gates.

He rained down various weapons and entrusted the mudrās; each and every mudrā was produced from the limbs and joints adorned with the marks of a Great Man by the Tathāgata, and is not something created through ritual action.

Why is this? Because within the adamantine essence (*vajra-kāya*), all is primordially complete; its nature is inherently firm and free from conceptual discrimination. It accomplishes sentient beings and can fulfill all aspirations: whether manifesting as the adamantine terror for subjugation, or manifesting as a bodhisattva endowed with great compassion, or manifesting as a celestial body so that ghosts and spirits are all subdued, or accomplishing activities by manifesting as the Karma-vajra—it can cause the practitioner to swiftly attain perfection.

The Tathāgatas of the five directions are placed upon the crown of the head, seated upon a great lotus within a full moon disc; like a great round mirror, it is transparent both inside and out, its essence devoid of self and other. This is the practitioner’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the instructional manual for the meaning of recitation within the wisdom of Amoghasiddhi.

The sequential method for the yoga offering of Vairocana-samādhi:
I take refuge in Buddha Vairocana, whose eyes of wondrous enlightenment open like lotus petals.
I now distinguish these corresponding dharmas, according to the essential sequence of their recitation and mindfulness;
may one rely upon this to swiftly achieve accomplishment, benefiting oneself and others while remaining far removed from dust and defilement.
Since this is the path set forth by those with the initial resolve, may all who mindfully apply skillful means be directed toward Bodhi.
Although the gateways for entering [the path] are immeasurable, none can surpass this one.

At that time, having received the *ācārya* initiation, the practitioner shall adorn a maṇḍala in a secluded place, smearing the ground with fragrant mud and making various offerings so as to make it utterly pure. He shall constantly keep his three karmas tranquil and undisturbed, give rise to a heart of compassion, and cause all sentient beings to attain total liberation. With single-minded devotion, he shall prostrate before the five maṇḍalas and visualize the assembly of holy ones as if they were present before his eyes.

Having sincerely repented of all transgressions, one then contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; one contemplates that the emptiness of all phenomena is primordially pure and free from any defilement or attachment.
Having reflected thus, he recites the secret mantra:
"Oṃ sarvabhāṣita-sarvadharma-sarvabhāṣita-tūṃ haṃ. He then performs the visualization of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*):
"The practitioner next cultivates *samādhi*, wherein the actions of body, speech, and mind pervade all of space."
Contemplating the three karmic gates of the Tathāgata, The profound teaching of the Vajra One Vehicle,
I rely upon the most supreme Yoga Dharma To reveal the gateway of mantras as they truly are;
Thus entering the Samaya of Samantabhadra, For my essence is identical to that of the Sattva-vajra.

One’s body resides within a lunar disc, identical to the *sattva*.
The mantra is as follows:
"Oṃ samayas tvam. One should visualize this body seated upon a pure moon disk, as if sitting upon the spread surface of a bright mirror.

extend the meditation, wisdom, generosity, and knowledge fingers straight upward.

next, one should open the heart and enter the Buddha’s wisdom, contemplating the syllable *tṛlaṭha* upon the breast.

Within the span of one cubit, upon an eight-petaled white lotus, the letter A appears vividly with the color of pure white light.

The mantra is as follows:

Mantra: "Oṃ (1) sunba ni-sunba hūṃ (2) hrīḥ-kṣiṇa hrīḥ-kṣiṇa hūṃ (3) hrīḥ-kṣiṇa āpaya hūṃ (4) ānaya ho bhagavan (5) mañjara hūṃ phaṭ (6). Next, bind the Lotus Family mudrā:
To bring about the accomplishment of *samādhi*, form the Vajra-bind with both hands of concentration and wisdom.
Generosity, wisdom, meditation, and knowledge are unified and established;
through these mantras and secret mudrās, the practice of samādhi swiftly manifests. The mantra is:
When a practitioner wishes to enter the Vajra-samādhi, they should first abide in the seal of the Wondrous Discerning Wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna).
With the two hands of concentration and wisdom joined palm-to-palm with fingers interlaced, the thumbs, ring fingers, middle fingers, and little fingers respectively support one another.
By cultivating meditative equipoise (samāhita) through this wondrous seal, one immediately attains the Tathāgata’s Immovable Wisdom (akṣobhya-jñāna).

The practitioner should next cultivate the practice of seated meditation with a clarified mind through the visualization of the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*). First, one must for one month discipline the body and mind, ensuring the mind becomes clear and pure; only then should one train in external deportment.
Furthermore, one should contemplate in this way: all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; all are free from both the grasper and the grasped, being ultimately pure and without any attachment.

Having reflected thus, he visualized all the Buddhas in the sky, complete with their primary and secondary marks, as numerous as motes of dust pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Extending their golden hands, they snapped their fingers and addressed him, saying:
"O son of good family!
One should observe the nature of one’s own mind through samādhi and bring it to accomplishment; thus, one should contemplate one’s own mind.
Before each of the Buddhas, prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground and take refuge with single-minded devotion, reciting the mantra:

"Oṃ cit-prativedha vaidhurya-kāruṇi. This is called the inner realization of untainted purity, the ultimate pinnacle, which leads to awakening into the ocean of all-knowledge and becoming equal to all Buddhas. This dharma is secret and must not be heard by those who are unprepared.
When wishing to enter meditative observation, recite this mantra:
"Oṃ samayam sattvaṃ. Having recited this secret word, one will immediately become fully endowed with all the pure vows and great merits of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, contemplate the syllable *vaṃ* as perfectly pure and signless; settle the mind upon this syllable and do not conceptualize any signs whatsoever. One’s own mind becomes concentrated, pure, and luminous, transparent both internally and externally, with no distinction between self and other.
When about to enter into meditative contemplation, recite the mantra:
"Oṃ bodhicitta-utpādayāmi. This causes the moon of the visualized mind to gradually expand and pervade the entire dharmadhātu.
The mantra is: "Oṃ tiṣṭha mañjula.

Having recited this mantra, one is able to cause the moon of the visualized mind to gradually expand until it pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Throughout all kalpas of the past and future limits, within every atom and every hair-pore, there are the assemblies at the bodhimandas of all Buddhas, as infinitely layered as Indra’s net.
One who performs this contemplation shall realize the profound wisdom of a bodhisattva.
The mantra is: *Oṃ cittapratividdhānugame*.

It enables the practitioner to swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi and to possess the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of all Buddhas. It flows forth from within the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*); it is not a manifestation produced by ritual action. Like a skilled *cintāmaṇi* gem that fulfills all wishes, it is spoken with one voice by all Buddhas.

At the time of contemplation, there is only luminous clarity; neither body nor mind is perceived, let alone any single object. Furthermore, do not conceive of this as emptiness, for it is called "like space" because of the absence of discursive thought and so forth, yet phenomena are not empty. If one practices until long and thoroughly matured, one shall realize this for oneself.
When performing this visualization, recite the secret mantra:

*Oṃ vajra-maṇḍala-praveśaya me*. By recollecting this vidyā-mantra, one is immediately able to realize and enter the stage of all consecration maṇḍalas, and may proceed at will and without obstruction through the secret dharma-gates of all bodhisattvas.

When performing this contemplation, there is no need for haste or delay; the essential point lies in realizing entry. If one can bring each [aspect] into correspondence with the mind, then great accomplishment will ensue. At all times and in all places, through intentional application, they will spontaneously correspond without obstruction. All delusive thoughts, such as greed, hatred, and ignorance, will not arise naturally without needing to be severed, as their nature is eternally pure.

This true Dharma-gate is the intrinsically pure mind of all sentient beings; whether as the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, from the Buddhas above down to ordinary beings below, it is entirely equal and without increase or decrease. It is only because it is shrouded by ignorance and deluded conceptualization that its essential nature is unable to manifest.

One who practices this contemplation realizes the samādhi of liberation and omniscience; this is termed the stage of the three virtuous ones prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*). All their actions spontaneously accord with reality, and they naturally enter the first ground, giving rise to great joy.
The reason for this is that taking the observation of the moon as a skillful means possesses three meanings:
first, the meaning of natural purity, because it is free from the defilement of desire;
second, the meaning of coolness, because it is free from the feverish affliction of hatred.
Third is the meaning of luminosity, because it is free from the darkness of ignorance.

Therefore, although the moon is taken as a metaphor, one must not understand it as being the actual moon. The worldly moon is composed of the four great elements and is ultimately subject to destruction; however, the self-nature of sentient beings—the pure mind—is without arising or ceasing. This is the internal realization of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and is not a realm known by those of the two vehicles, Śrāvakas, or non-Buddhists.
For one who practices this contemplation, all Buddha-dharmas and their merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are realized not through another.
This single dharma encompasses immeasurable dharmas; moment by moment, one awakens to and enters into them with sovereign non-obstruction, gradually ascending from stage to stage.

Those who study this contemplation must not exclusively cling to non-thought as the ultimate goal; rather, they must employ right mindfulness to advance through skillful means, and only then will they realize entry into the ultimately pure ocean of Dharma.
In order to cause entry into the stage of Buddhahood, one should form the Vajrasamaya mudrā:
with the ten fingers fully extended and crossed at the outer edges, the thumbs and ring fingers held upright like banners.
Placing it upon the heart, forehead, throat, and crown, recite [the mantra] once for each to perform the consecration.
The mantra says:
One should visualize all the Tathāgatas holding precious maṇi jewels and sprinkling them upon my crown;
with the union of concentration and wisdom, one forms the vajra-bond, while the fingers of effort, strength, meditation, and wisdom take the shape of jewels.
Having performed the empowerment upon the forehead with the mudrā, the crown of the five buddhas' wisdom is placed upon his head;
then, separating the *jñānamuṣṭi* (wisdom-fist), it circles behind the head.
Having completed the circumambulation, the mantra for binding is recited as follows:

"Oṃ mārāra-danna abhiṣiñca māṃ sarva-māra-mardane nirdhūta-guṇa vajra-kavace namaḥ. The practitioner should further reflect thus: "I have now attained perfect enlightenment; I shall arouse great compassion for all sentient beings. Within the inexhaustible cycle of birth and death, I shall constantly don the armor of the great vow.

Desiring to purify the Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, and having served all the Tathāgatas, I shall cause all sentient beings to sit beneath the Bodhi tree, subdue the celestial Māras, and attain supreme perfect enlightenment. Therefore, I must don the armor of the compassion of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time."
Having recited this secret mantra, one rotates the thumbs and forefingers against each other three times in a circle; then, uttering the syllable Oṃ,
one visualizes the syllable Oṃ on the thumb and the syllable Caṃ on the forefinger.
Visualize a blue cord as if it were a breastplate being fastened:
first around the chest, back, navel, and waist;
then with three turns spiraling upward from the ribs to the top, and finally looping back toward the throat.
Returning to the space behind the crown, it circles three times back and forth across the forehead;
having reached the area behind the crown, it descends evenly before the altar and the wisdom [deities].
This is the Vajra Armor.
"Oṃ vajrakavaca vajrakīla vajraparighāta. Next, one should form the mudrā of joy:
strike the two hands of concentration and wisdom together three times; by the empowerment of this mudrā of joy, all the noble hosts shall rejoice.
The mantra is: "Oṃ vajraduḥkhānta.
